title: Did Archimedes Really Run Naked Shouting Eureka?
description:
Everyone has heard it: Archimedes figured it out in the bath and ran naked through the streets shouting Eureka. This episode tells only what the records show. The earliest text we can find is the preface to Book IX of Ten Books on Architecture by the Roman architect Vitruvius, written in the late first century BC, nearly two centuries after Archimedes: King Hiero's gold crown, the craftsman accused of mixing in silver, the water spilling over in the bath, and "naked, homeward," shouting εὕρηκα ("I have found it") all the way. Archimedes' surviving works, On Floating Bodies included, say not a word about a crown or a bath. Plutarch also tells of the bath and the cry "I have found it," but mentions no clothes and no going home; an anonymous Latin poem from the late Roman Empire has the gold crown but no bath, and uses a balance in water. In 1586 Galileo, in his early twenties, called the water method "crude and far from exact" in a short essay shown only to friends and not printed until 1644. Mathematician Chris Rorres estimates the water level differs by just 0.41 mm, while a balance in water is off by 13 g.

Limits: the text says "homeward," not "into the street" or "forgot his clothes"; Rorres's numbers rest on a case he assumed (1 kg, 30% silver, a 20 cm opening); no one can prove the story false, so this case stays open. Sources are in the references below.

Illustrations are AI-generated; historical figures are unnamed cartoon characters, not likenesses; modern researchers are not drawn.

Information as of 2026-10-20

ar101.text: Third century BC, Syracuse: a man walks into a public bathhouse.

ar102.text: A hard problem is on his mind.

ar103.text: At the pool's edge, he slowly lowers himself in.

ar104.text: He notices: the deeper his body sinks, the more water spills over the edge.

ar106.text: What did he realize in that moment?

ar108.text: a Roman architect wrote this scene nearly two centuries later,

ar109.text: and his point wasn't Archimedes at all.

ar111.text: Over a century later, a retelling of the bath lacks one thing.

ar112.text: About 1,800 years after Archimedes, a man in his early twenties read about the water method

ar113.text: and opened a short essay with harsh words.

ar114.text: Did he really run naked in the street yelling Eureka?

ar201.text: The earliest text we can find on the nakedness is in that Roman architect's book.

ar202.text: He is Vitruvius; his Ten Books on Architecture, for Augustus, date to the late 1st century BC.

ar232.text: Where did he hear this story?

ar233.text: The book doesn't say a word.

ar203.text: It opens Book Nine: King Hiero of Syracuse, newly in power,

ar204.text: vowed to offer a gold crown to a temple.

ar205.text: Call it a crown; it was really a wreath of gold leaves.

ar206.text: The king weighed out gold for a craftsman;

ar207.text: it came back at the exact weight.

ar208.text: But someone claimed the craftsman kept some gold and mixed in the same weight of silver.

ar209.text: Yet it was meant for the gods: no melting it, no scraping it.

ar210.text: Unable to expose it, the king asked Archimedes.

ar211.text: That troubled man walking into the bathhouse at the start? This was him.

ar212.text: The overflow showed him how to expose the fraud.

ar213.text: Not waiting a moment, he leapt from the pool for joy,

ar214.text: and headed home naked, shouting as he ran:

ar215.text: Eureka, Eureka! Meaning: I have found it.

ar228.text: So did he run naked down the street?

ar216.text: The text says "homeward," not into the street;

ar217.text: "Forgot his clothes" and "ran all over town" were added later.

ar229.text: As for "naked": the Latin word sometimes means wearing just a tunic;

ar230.text: but he'd just leapt out of the bath, so the most natural literal reading is naked.

ar219.text: Vitruvius goes on: reportedly he made gold and silver lumps, each the crown's weight,

ar220.text: put each in a brimming vessel, and measured how much water it took to refill it.

ar221.text: The crown displaced more water than equal-weight gold: the silver was exposed.

ar222.text: The craftsman's fate? Not recorded; the story stops there.

ar223.text: But why tell this story in a book on architecture?

ar224.text: Because Book Nine opens with a protest on behalf of writers:

ar225.text: writers deserve the honors athletes get, and more.

ar226.text: Archimedes is one of his examples.

ar227.text: And the hero himself? Did Archimedes ever write about the wreath?

ar301.text: In his surviving works, at least, not a word on a crown or a bathtub.

ar302.text: Some of his books were lost; some, by luck, survived.

ar303.text: One, On Floating Bodies, is about exactly that: things put in water.

ar304.text: It says a body heavier than water weighs less in water,

ar305.text: less by exactly the weight of water it displaces.

ar306.text: That's what we call buoyancy; he was talking about weighing in water.

ar307.text: The overflow at the start compares volume, not the principle in this book.

ar308.text: How did other ancient writers tell of the bath?

ar309.text: The version from over a century later is by the Greek writer Plutarch.

ar310.text: He writes: bathing, Archimedes saw the overflow and worked out how to measure the crown;

ar311.text: as if possessed, he leapt out and went off, shouting "I have found it!"

ar322.text: Plutarch prefaces it with "they say": by his time it was already a story going around.

ar312.text: The missing thing is the nakedness: Plutarch says not a word about clothes,

ar313.text: nor that he went home; the word he uses is "walk," not "run."

ar314.text: A bath, but no nakedness; is there a version the other way round?

ar315.text: Yes. An anonymous Latin poem from the late Roman Empire clearly tells the same story:

ar316.text: Sicily's king, a gold crown for the gods, a smith who added silver: all there;

ar317.text: but no bath, and no "I have found it";

ar318.text: not even Archimedes' name, just "the master of Syracuse."

ar319.text: The poem uses a balance: equal weights of gold and silver on each side, level,

ar320.text: then both lowered into water; the moment they go in, the gold side sinks.

ar321.text: One crown: measure the water, or weigh it. Which really works?

ar401.text: The water method was knocked as early as 1586.

ar402.text: By that young man in his early twenties: Italy's Galileo.

ar403.text: He wrote a short essay later called The Little Balance; it begins:

ar404.text: As some write, sinking the crown to tell gold from silver by how the water rises

ar405.text: is, frankly, very crude and far from exact.

ar406.text: So where did the water part come from?

ar407.text: His guess: word spread Archimedes caught a thief with water;

ar420.text: a writer of that time wrote it down,

ar408.text: and, to stretch the little he'd heard, added the water method himself.

ar409.text: We think it's the best line in this whole file.

ar411.text: But it's his guess, not proof; and he doubted only the method, not the bath.

ar412.text: So what did he think Archimedes really used?

ar413.text: A balance. Like that poem: weighing in water.

ar414.text: Remember On Floating Bodies? Galileo said this is the method Archimedes would use,

ar415.text: since it rests on what that very book proved.

ar419.text: But how far off was the water method, really?

ar501.text: Mathematician Rorres did the math: a 1 kg wreath with 30% of its gold swapped for silver,

ar502.text: and a container 20 cm across at the mouth.

ar503.text: Put in the wreath, then equal-weight gold: the levels differ by only:

ar504.text: 0.41 millimeters, less than half a millimeter.

ar505.text: And a balance, weighing in water?

ar506.text: The sides differ by 13 grams; easy, he says, for scales of Archimedes' day to detect.

ar507.text: In 2006 he told Scientific American the water method works in theory;

ar508.text: but try it for real, and reality gets in the way.

ar509.text: So the method probably fails; what about the bath and the "I have found it"?

ar510.text: Rorres says the story may hold some truth: Archimedes did measure the volume of things;

ar511.text: but the "I have found it" moment may have come from discovering buoyancy,

ar512.text: not from a tub and a naked dash down the street.

ar513.text: So, the opening question: did he really run naked in the street yelling Eureka?

ar514.text: The naked run home survives in one record only, by that Roman architect;

ar515.text: whether it happened, no evidence can say.

ar517.text: In the story you grew up with, did he run out dressed?

ar518.text: We tell only what the records show; subscribe to open files with us.
